questions.question: What condition on $A$ is required before Cramer’s rule can be used?
In Cramer’s rule, how is $B_j$ formed?
What does Cramer’s rule express?
options: Every rectangular system as a row echelon matrix.
The determinant as the sum of all unknowns.
Each unknown of a square linear system as a quotient of determinants.
The kernel of a linear map directly, without solving equations

questions.question: What is the denominator in $x_j=\det(B_j)/\det(A)$?
Why does Cramer’s rule give a unique solution?
options: Replacing a column always makes a determinant equal to $1$.
Every system of equations has a unique solution.
The nonsingularity of $A$ ensures uniqueness for $Ax=b$.
The right-hand side vector is never zero.

options: Replace rows instead of columns to avoid the zero
None; the rule cannot be used because the denominator is zero.
Set every unknown equal to zero.

questions.question: If $\det(A)=-3$ and $\det(B_2)=6$, what is $x_2$?
Why does Cramer’s rule replace a column rather than a row?
options: Replacing rows would always preserve the determinant.
Rows of $A$ are never involved in linear systems.

questions.question: What should make you reject Cramer’s rule immediately for a system?
Why is Cramer’s rule considered an explicit formula rather than an elimination procedure?
options: It solves only by back substitution.
It writes each coordinate directly as a determinant quotient.
It guesses the unknowns and checks them.
It performs row operations until RREF is reached.

Cramer's rule changes singular systems into nonsingular ones

Singular systems always have exactly one solution.

questions.question: Cramer's rule solves $Ax=b$ using $n$ determinants of $n\times n$ matrices. Why is this impractical for large $n$?
options: It applies only to homogeneous systems.
